content: 1. A 2016 Cochrane review indicated that responsive feeding in infants led to slower weight gain but reduced the time required for transitioning from enteral tube feeding to oral feeding. 2. Another systematic review reported that responsive feeding decreased the length of hospitalization and increased weight gain in infants. 3. In 2011, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended that low-birth-weight (LBW) infants who are orally fed but not breastfed should be fed based on their hunger cues, except when the infant remains asleep for more than three hours since the last feed. 4. Evidence on the effectiveness of responsive feeding versus scheduled feeding was derived from a systematic review of eight randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 455 preterm or LBW infants from Canada, Iran, Israel, and the USA. 5. These studies were conducted in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs), where health workers, rather than families, implemented either scheduled or responsive feeding protocols. 6. Scheduled feeding regimens typically involved feeding every 2–3 hours, with volumes ranging from 120 to 180 ml/kg per day. 7. The duration of the interventions varied, with a minimum of three days and a maximum lasting until hospital discharge. 8. Only one study included very preterm infants (<32 weeks’ gestation), while the others focused on preterm infants. 9. Seven studies assessed growth outcomes, including weight gain, but none evaluated mortality, morbidity, or neurodevelopmental outcomes. 10. Families expressed a desire to be involved in the care of their infants, including decisions about feeding methods and nutritional support. 11. No specific evidence was found regarding whether families preferred responsive feeding over scheduled feeding for their preterm or LBW infants or whether they found one method more acceptable than the other. 12. In healthcare facilities, infants born before 34 weeks’ gestation can be fed every 2–3 hours, while those born at 34 weeks or later can be fed every 3–4 hours or using responsive feeding. 13. At home, feeding schedules can be determined collaboratively by families and healthcare workers based on clinical judgment and preferences. 14. National or local guidelines should be used to guide infrastructure, equipment, and supplies for healthcare facilities. 15. Health workers at all levels can support mothers and families in feeding practices, and standardized training, supervision, and monitoring packages are necessary. 16. Responsive feeding requires careful observation of the infant’s behavior and is more commonly implemented in well-staffed NICUs and special care nurseries. 17. There is no specific evidence on the feasibility and equity of responsive versus scheduled feeding for preterm or LBW infants. 18. WHO recommends that preterm or LBW infants should be exclusively breastfed until six months of age, despite very-low-certainty evidence, due to the potential harms of less than six months of exclusive breastfeeding. 19. A systematic review of 42 studies involving 89,638 infants showed consistent harm from the use of infant formula, particularly an increased risk of necrotizing enterocolitis, with no evidence of benefit over exclusive breastfeeding. 20. Exclusive breastfeeding until six months is the standard of care for preterm and LBW infants in many countries and forms the foundation of national policies and programs. 21. Mothers should be encouraged and supported to provide their own breast milk, including colostrum, for their infants. 22. WHO defines exclusive breastfeeding as feeding no other foods or fluids (not even water) except breast milk, medicines, vitamins, and minerals. 23. Preterm and LBW infants are more vulnerable to nutritional deficiencies, and the risks of contamination from complementary foods and early formula feeding are well-documented. 24. Evidence on the effectiveness of exclusive breastfeeding for less than six months versus six months was derived from two RCTs involving 307 preterm or LBW infants in Honduras and India. 25. One trial in Honduras randomized term small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants to receive nutrient-rich complementary foods starting at four months of age. 26. The other trial in India randomized infants born before 34 weeks’ gestation to receive complementary foods starting at four months corrected age. 27. For exclusive breastfeeding less than six months compared to six months, one trial reported morbidity outcomes (percentage of days with diarrhea and/or fever), two trials reported growth outcomes (weight gain, weight-for-age z-scores, and length gain), and one trial reported neurodevelopmental outcomes (time to achieve motor developmental milestones). 28. No trials reported mortality outcomes. 29. Families expressed concerns about providing their own milk after returning home, citing challenges such as balancing work commitments, maternity leave, nighttime feeding, and partner support. 30. Families also expressed concerns about infant formula, including nutrient composition, water supply, contamination, and cost, but valued having formula available if circumstances required it. 31. Promotion of exclusive breastfeeding for six months should be integrated into national programs and occur throughout the antenatal and postnatal periods. 32. Health workers at all levels can promote exclusive breastfeeding for six months, but no specific evidence was found on the feasibility and equity of exclusive breastfeeding for preterm or LBW infants. 33. Enteral iron supplementation and feed advancement should be based on clinical judgment, with fast feed advancement defined as increments of up to 30 ml/kg per day. 34. Further research is needed to understand the neurodevelopmental effects of fast feed advancement. 35. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) emphasized the need for shared decision-making with parents, including informing them about the benefits and risks of feeding practices and the need for further research. 36. Trials comparing fast and slow feed advancement showed no significant differences in mortality, necrotizing enterocolitis, sepsis, weight gain, or head circumference, but moderate-certainty evidence suggested a reduction in time to regain birth weight and length of hospital stay with fast advancement. 37. Exclusive breastfeeding for six months remains a strong recommendation due to its potential benefits and alignment with global standards of care.
